newsitem.title: USA: Britain, Ireland agree on N Ireland disarmament.
newsitem.headline: Britain, Ireland agree on N Ireland disarmament.

text.p: Britain and Ireland on Monday agreed a joint stance on guerrilla disarmament that could pave the way for progress in deadlocked Northern Ireland peace talks.
British Prime Minister Tony Blair and Irish Prime Minister John Bruton announced the understanding after a meeting at the United Nations on the fringes of an environmental summit.

But Blair was careful not to fan expectations of a breakthrough in one of the world's longest-running guerrilla conflicts, which has claimed the lives of more than 3,200 people over the last 28 years.
"I think it's possible that we have the basis of a way forward. But of course this has got to be agreed with all the other parties," he told reporters.
Blair's comments corrected the thrust of earlier remarks by one of his aides, who said no agreement had been reached between the Dublin and London governments.

"We want to try and make sure that we can move this process forward, but it can't just be done by the British and Irish governments talking to each other. There's got to be other people involved too," Blair said.
Bruton, more upbeat, told Irish network RTE that the agreement would create conditions for rapid movement in multi-party peace talks taking place in Belfast.

He said all possible clarification had now been provided to Sinn Fein, the political wing of the IRA, which now had to choose between the political path and the dual approach of political action and violence that it had been pursuing.

RTE said the accord dealt with ways to bring about the disarmament of the Irish Republican Army (IRA), fighting to end British rule in Northern Ireland, if the guerrillas renewed a 17-month truce it broke in February 1996.

An Anglo-Irish paper aimed at ending a 17-month stalemate between Protestant and Catholic politicians at the Belfast talks on "arms decommissioning" was expected to be tabled on Tuesday, political sources said.

They said the Anglo-Irish way forward was likely to mirror proposals by the talks' chairman, former U.S. senator George Mitchell, for the issue to be tackled alongside negotiations on other political matters.

British officials said Blair was cautious because of fears that any formula for scrapping IRA arms acceptable to Catholic politicians would be instinctively rejected by Protestants who want Northern Ireland to remain part of Britain.

"It isn't just the Britsh and Irish governments talking to each other. There are other parties that have to be involved, too, and there are all sorts of discussions that have to take place," Blair said.
He said he hoped to be able to make a statement to parliament on Wednesday that would take stock of the peace process, including the question of decommissioning.
"I am desperate to do everything I can to get a lasting peace and political settlement in Northern Ireland," Blair stressed. "We have got a responsibility to try and do everything we can..."
Earlier Sinn Fein's chief negotiator, Martin McGuinness, had said the disarmament issue remained a major stumbling block in peace efforts.
He said Sinn Fein wanted an end to violence in the province and the start of real peace negotiations.

"We are working day and night...trying to move the situation forward, and to convince the British government and others that the decommissioning issue which has blocked this process must be removed as an obstacle to forward movement," he told BBC radio.
